content.content: {"result":"{\"success\": true, \"data\": {\"stdout\": \"# Discussion (Draft)\\n\\n## Training-time vs Inference-time Structural Information\\n\\nA growing body of work integrates structural code information into retrieval and localization systems, but the *stage* at which structural information is consumed differs fundamentally across methods. CodexGraph (Liu et al., NAACL 2025) materializes a code property graph in a Neo4j database and exposes a Cypher query interface that an LLM agent invokes at inference time; each query triggers multiple rounds of LLM-guided graph traversal, incurring latency proportional to task complexity. LocAgent (Chen et al., ACL 2025) similarly constructs a directed heterogeneous graph with call, import, and inheritance edges, achieving 92.7% file-level localization on SWE-bench-Lite—but again through multi-turn LLM inference over the graph at query time. RANGER (Shah et al., 2025) and RepoGraph (Ouyang et al., ICLR 2025) follow the same paradigm: runtime graph construction and traversal with per-query computational cost that scales linearly with query volume. [源: plan_017]\\n\\nStructFuse takes a different approach by amortizing all structural computation into the training phase. We perform bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis (2-hop call-graph scope) via CodeQL as a one-time extraction step—approximately 8.9 seconds per instance, totaling ~110 hours for 44K instances with zero timeouts—and use the resulting connectivity information exclusively for hard negative mining during contrastive training. At inference time, the trained encoder operates at standard embedding speed with no graph overhead. This design makes StructFuse suited for latency-sensitive, high-throughput retrieval scenarios where per-query graph traversal would be prohibitive. [源: m1_extraction / plan_006]\\n\\nThe two paradigms are complementary rather than competing. A StructFuse-trained encoder, whose representations already encode data-flow semantics, can serve as a first-stage retriever that narrows the candidate set before an inference-time graph agent (e.g., LocAgent or CodexGraph) performs targeted structural reranking. Evaluating such hybrid pipelines is a natural direction for future work. We note that direct numerical comparison between StructFuse and inference-time graph methods is methodologically challenging: they address different task interfaces (embedding-based ranked retrieval vs. multi-turn agentic localization) and have been evaluated on different benchmarks under different metrics. [源: plan_017]\\n\\n## Inter-procedural vs Intra-procedural Scope\\n\\nAmong methods that incorporate data-flow or control-flow analysis, scope varies considerably. GraphCoder (Liu et al., ASE 2024) constructs a Code Context Graph combining control-flow, control-dependence, and data-dependence subgraphs—the closest to StructFuse in leveraging data-flow semantics—but its analysis is strictly intra-procedural: no information crosses function boundaries. ARISE (Seddik & Fard, 2026) performs repository-level graph construction with data-flow edges, yet its data-flow analysis is also intra-procedural, limited to within-function def-use chains, with cross-function relationships captured only through structural edges (call, inheritance). CodexGraph and LocAgent capture call graphs and inheritance hierarchies but model no data-flow semantics at all—edges represent syntactic relationships (who calls whom), not how values propagate. [源: plan_017]\\n\\nStructFuse occupies a middle ground: bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis with a 2-hop call-graph scope. This design crosses function boundaries to capture indirect data dependencies (e.g., a value defined in function A that flows through function B to affect function C) while remaining computationally tractable. Our plan_006 analysis shows that 2-hop scoping covers Z=40.8% of query-candidate pairs with structural connectivity, with median coverage reaching 96% for extra-large repositories where inter-procedural dependencies are most prevalent. The bounding trades completeness for scalability: deeper call chains (>2 hops) are truncated, but the resulting extraction completes with 0% timeout rate across 123 repositories. Exploring larger hop bounds (3-hop and beyond) via plan_007 ablation remains a direction for future investigation. [源: plan_006 / m1_extraction]\\n\\n## Limitations\\n\\n**Bounded inter-procedural scope.** The 2-hop call-graph bounding in our CodeQL extraction truncates data-flow paths that traverse more than two function boundaries. While 2-hop coverage reaches Z=40.8% overall and is high for large repositories (median 96% for XL repos), deep call chains characteristic of certain architectural patterns (e.g., deeply layered middleware stacks, recursive visitor patterns) may be incompletely captured. The planned hop-count ablation (plan_007) will quantify the marginal value of extending the analysis boundary, though we expect diminishing returns as longer paths introduce noise from increasingly indirect dependencies. [���: plan_006]\\n\\n**Language and tooling constraints.** Our structural extraction relies on CodeQL, which supports a fixed set of languages (Python, Java, JavaScript, C/C++, Go, Ruby, C#, Swift). For languages outside this set, alternative static analysis frameworks (e.g., tree-sitter for syntax, Joern for data-flow) would be required, and the quality of bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis may differ. The method's core principle—using structural connectivity for training-time negative mining—is language-agnostic, but the specific extraction pipeline is not. [源: m1_extraction]\\n\\n**Structural data coverage.** In the current M1 extraction, 36% of instances yield structural data, meaning 64% lack data-flow connectivity information and fall back to non-structural negative mining strategies. This rate reflects runtime extraction failures rather than a fundamental limitation of the approach; a planned re-extraction (m1_reextract_v2) with improved error handling is expected to raise coverage substantially. Nonetheless, even at full coverage, instances from small or self-contained repositories may genuinely lack inter-procedural data-flow paths, limiting the applicability of structure-grounded negatives for those cases. [源: m1_extraction / registry]\\n\\n**Statistical power.** Our current results are based on n=3 random seeds per configuration, yielding df=2 for pairwise comparisons. This limits statistical power and increases Type II error risk—observed effect sizes (+1.6–2.0pp R@1 for embedding mining, +0.8–2.3pp for dataflow negatives on Qwen) may not reach conventional significance thresholds. The full M2 experimental matrix (9 seeds × 3 strategies × 2 encoders) is in progress and will provide adequate power for bootstrap confidence interval estimation. Until then, we characterize our findings as observed patterns with mechanistic support rather than statistically confirmed effects. [源: m2_full / plan_016]\\n\", \"stderr\": \"\", \"return_code\": 0}, \"error\": null, \"metadata\": {\"elapsed_seconds\": 0.97}}"}

{"success": true, "data": {"stdout": "# Discussion (Draft)

## Training-time vs Inference-time Structural Information

A growing body of work integrates structural code information into retrieval and localization systems, but the *stage* at which structural information is consumed differs fundamentally across methods. CodexGraph (Liu et al., NAACL 2025) materializes a code property graph in a Neo4j database and exposes a Cypher query interface that an LLM agent invokes at inference time; each query triggers multiple rounds of LLM-guided graph traversal, incurring latency proportional to task complexity. LocAgent (Chen et al., ACL 2025) similarly constructs a directed heterogeneous graph with call, import, and inheritance edges, achieving 92.7% file-level localization on SWE-bench-Lite—but again through multi-turn LLM inference over the graph at query time. RANGER (Shah et al., 2025) and RepoGraph (Ouyang et al., ICLR 2025) follow the same paradigm: runtime graph construction and traversal with per-query computational cost that scales linearly with query volume. [源: plan_017]

StructFuse takes a different approach by amortizing all structural computation into the training phase. We perform bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis (2-hop call-graph scope) via CodeQL as a one-time extraction step—approximately 8.9 seconds per instance, totaling ~110 hours for 44K instances with zero timeouts—and use the resulting connectivity information exclusively for hard negative mining during contrastive training. At inference time, the trained encoder operates at standard embedding speed with no graph overhead. This design makes StructFuse suited for latency-sensitive, high-throughput retrieval scenarios where per-query graph traversal would be prohibitive. [源: m1_extraction / plan_006]

The two paradigms are complementary rather than competing. A StructFuse-trained encoder, whose representations already encode data-flow semantics, can serve as a first-stage retriever that narrows the candidate set before an inference-time graph agent (e.g., LocAgent or CodexGraph) performs targeted structural reranking. Evaluating such hybrid pipelines is a natural direction for future work. We note that direct numerical comparison between StructFuse and inference-time graph methods is methodologically challenging: they address different task interfaces (embedding-based ranked retrieval vs. multi-turn agentic localization) and have been evaluated on different benchmarks under different metrics. [源: plan_017]

## Inter-procedural vs Intra-procedural Scope

Among methods that incorporate data-flow or control-flow analysis, scope varies considerably. GraphCoder (Liu et al., ASE 2024) constructs a Code Context Graph combining control-flow, control-dependence, and data-dependence subgraphs—the closest to StructFuse in leveraging data-flow semantics—but its analysis is strictly intra-procedural: no information crosses function boundaries. ARISE (Seddik & Fard, 2026) performs repository-level graph construction with data-flow edges, yet its data-flow analysis is also intra-procedural, limited to within-function def-use chains, with cross-function relationships captured only through structural edges (call, inheritance). CodexGraph and LocAgent capture call graphs and inheritance hierarchies but model no data-flow semantics at all—edges represent syntactic relationships (who calls whom), not how values propagate. [源: plan_017]

StructFuse occupies a middle ground: bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis with a 2-hop call-graph scope. This design crosses function boundaries to capture indirect data dependencies (e.g., a value defined in function A that flows through function B to affect function C) while remaining computationally tractable. Our plan_006 analysis shows that 2-hop scoping covers Z=40.8% of query-candidate pairs with structural connectivity, with median coverage reaching 96% for extra-large repositories where inter-procedural dependencies are most prevalent. The bounding trades completeness for scalability: deeper call chains (>2 hops) are truncated, but the resulting extraction completes with 0% timeout rate across 123 repositories. Exploring larger hop bounds (3-hop and beyond) via plan_007 ablation remains a direction for future investigation. [源: plan_006 / m1_extraction]

## Limitations

**Bounded inter-procedural scope.** The 2-hop call-graph bounding in our CodeQL extraction truncates data-flow paths that traverse more than two function boundaries. While 2-hop coverage reaches Z=40.8% overall and is high for large repositories (median 96% for XL repos), deep call chains characteristic of certain architectural patterns (e.g., deeply layered middleware stacks, recursive visitor patterns) may be incompletely captured. The planned hop-count ablation (plan_007) will quantify the marginal value of extending the analysis boundary, though we expect diminishing returns as longer paths introduce noise from increasingly indirect dependencies. [���: plan_006]

**Language and tooling constraints.** Our structural extraction relies on CodeQL, which supports a fixed set of languages (Python, Java, JavaScript, C/C++, Go, Ruby, C#, Swift). For languages outside this set, alternative static analysis frameworks (e.g., tree-sitter for syntax, Joern for data-flow) would be required, and the quality of bounded inter-procedural data-flow analysis may differ. The method's core principle—using structural connectivity for training-time negative mining—is language-agnostic, but the specific extraction pipeline is not. [源: m1_extraction]

**Structural data coverage.** In the current M1 extraction, 36% of instances yield structural data, meaning 64% lack data-flow connectivity information and fall back to non-structural negative mining strategies. This rate reflects runtime extraction failures rather than a fundamental limitation of the approach; a planned re-extraction (m1_reextract_v2) with improved error handling is expected to raise coverage substantially. Nonetheless, even at full coverage, instances from small or self-contained repositories may genuinely lack inter-procedural data-flow paths, limiting the applicability of structure-grounded negatives for those cases. [源: m1_extraction / registry]

**Statistical power.** Our current results are based on n=3 random seeds per configuration, yielding df=2 for pairwise comparisons. This limits statistical power and increases Type II error risk—observed effect sizes (+1.6–2.0pp R@1 for embedding mining, +0.8–2.3pp for dataflow negatives on Qwen) may not reach conventional significance thresholds. The full M2 experimental matrix (9 seeds × 3 strategies × 2 encoders) is in progress and will provide adequate power for bootstrap confidence interval estimation. Until then, we characterize our findings as observed patterns with mechanistic support rather than statistically confirmed effects. [源: m2_full / plan_016]
